Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation

Yuheng Chen ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology Email: yuheng.chen@student.kit.edu    Yufan Chen ††thanks: Corresponding author: Yufan Chen (yufan.chen@kit.edu). Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology Email: yufan.chen@kit.edu    Zhuojun Cai Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology    Ruiping Liu Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology    Junwei Zheng Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology    Jiale Wei Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology    Di Wen Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology    Weijia Fan Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology Affiliation: University of Alberta    Kunyu Peng Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology    Jiaming Zhang Affiliation: Hunan University    Rainer Stiefelhagen Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology
Abstract

Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at RPD Project.

1 Introduction

Scientific documents are not just sequences of recognized words. A single page may contain two-column prose, section headers, equations, tables, figures, captions, footnotes, author metadata, and visual evidence whose meaning is not recoverable from optical character recognition (OCR) alone. Document AI has therefore progressed through layout analysis Xu et al. (2020); Xu et al. (2021); Huang et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2024), table recognition Zhong et al. (2020), document VQA Kim et al. (2022), OCR-free parsing Wei et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2025), and multimodal document models Ye et al. (2023). In accessibility and machine-readable paper ingestion, the useful output is not an isolated layout map or a free-form page summary, but a structured page representation that can be read, reflowed, indexed, and audited.

Existing benchmarks usually evaluate pieces of this representation in isolation. Layout datasets measure region localization Zhong et al. (2019); Li et al. (2020); Pfitzmann et al. (2022), OCR and table benchmarks Smock et al. (2022) measure textual structure, reading-order datasets Wang et al. (2021b) focus on sequencing, captioning, and alt-text datasets Sharma et al. (2018); Srivatsan et al. (2024) describe isolated or context-conditioned images. These tasks are necessary, but they do not test whether a system can produce a single consistent parse in which boxes, labels, reading order, text, tables, captions, and visual descriptions agree with each other. This gap is particularly visible in scientific PDFs, where captions frequently refer to nearby figures or tables, equations interrupt prose, and visual elements carry technical information that should be exposed to downstream readers.

We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified task and dataset for unified document parsing with visual element description generation as shown in Fig. 1. Given a page image, a model must output an ordered list of elements, which includes a bounding box, semantic category, reading-order index, recognized text content, an explicit caption link when applicable, and an alternative-text description for visual elements. The key novelty is not any single field, but enforcing their agreement in one auditable page parse. The unified output contract can be implemented by either end-to-end models or modular systems. The benchmark contains 2,402 open-access scientific documents, 18,164 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances.

Modern VLMs and document-specialized models Dosovitskiy et al. (2021); Li et al. (2023); Dai et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023b); Bai et al. (2023); Lv et al. (2023); Bai et al. (2025); Gemma Team et al. (2025) increasingly use frozen or partially frozen visual encoders. When such models merge visual tokens before generation, local spatial evidence can be weakened exactly where element extents, reading order, and caption-object alignment are required. We therefore introduce SARA, a lightweight Spatial Alignment Residual Adapter for end-to-end VLM parsing. SARA freezes the base VLM, reuses intermediate visual encoder layers, projects their concatenated features into the token space, aligns with crop-aware spatial grids, and injects into the native merged tokens. The task makes spatial-alignment failures measurable, while SARA tests a direct architectural response without changing labels or evaluation. To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a novel task and dataset for unified document parsing with alternative-text generation into a shared structured schema.

  • •

    We propose SARA, a Spatial Alignment Residual Adapter that injects crop-aware spatial cues into VLM tokens to improve layout-sensitive document understanding.

  • •

    We establish a unified evaluation protocol covering both document parsing and alternative-text generation, enabling systematic assessment of parsing fidelity and generation quality.

  • •

    We conduct extensive experiments and ablation studies, showing that crop-aware spatial alignment consistently benefits unified document parsing and alternative-text generation.

2 Related Work

2.1 Document Layout and Parsing Datasets

Document-layout benchmarks have made document understanding measurable by isolating the output. Early resources, such as RVL-CDIP Harley et al. (2015), treat documents as classes, whereas FUNSD Jaume et al. (2019) focuses on form. CORD Park et al. (2019) and SROIE Huang et al. (2021) further show that domain-specific schemas enhance extraction but specialized. Similar to table, SciTSR Chi et al. (2019) targets scientific table structure, and PubTables-1M Smock et al. (2022) scales table recognition, but neither requires the table, caption, reading position, and visual description to agree in one element record. PubLayNet Zhong et al. (2019) made large-scale layout detection practical, and DocBank Li et al. (2020) expand token-level layout supervision. DocLayNet Pfitzmann et al. (2022) improved further with richer human annotations, while M6Doc Cheng et al. (2023) expanded layout analysis across heterogeneous documents. For robustness, RoDLA Chen et al. (2024) stresses layout robustness, whereas ReadingBank Wang et al. (2021b) isolates reading-order prediction. Broader evaluations such as DocVQA Mathew et al. (2021) and DUDE Van Landeghem et al. (2023) test document understanding through answers rather than page parses. OmniDocBench Ouyang et al. (2025) moves closer to document parsing, while MMLongBench-Doc Ma et al. (2024) stresses long-context document understanding.

2.2 Document VLMs and Pipeline Systems

Structure-aware representations are often precise, while generative systems are flexible but low performance. LayoutLM Xu et al. (2020) and LayoutLMv2 Xu et al. (2021) made layout-aware pretraining central for document understanding. LayoutLMv3 Huang et al. (2022) further unifies text and image modeling through task-specific heads rather than complete generator. DocFormer Appalaraju et al. (2021) and VGT Da et al. (2023) emphasize structure-aware encoding, reinforcing the explicit geometry. OCR-free generation such as Donut Kim et al. (2022) can emit structured text directly from an image, while Pix2Struct Lee et al. (2023) support screenshot-style pretraining. Nougat Blecher et al. (2023) specializes this generative view for academic documents, and GOT-OCR Wei et al. (2024) extends OCR-style generation toward broader text recognition. Recent document parsers push toward full-page extraction, e.g., DeepSeek-OCR Wei et al. (2025) uses visual compression for OCR, while Dolphin-v2 Feng et al. (2026) illustrates universal document parsing. MonkeyOCR Li et al. (2025) emphasizes structure-recognition-relation decomposition, and PaddleOCR-VL Cui et al. (2025a) targets compact multilingual document parsing. MinerU Wang et al. (2024) takes a more inspectable pipeline route. General VLMs provide another axis of flexibility, e.g., BLIP-2 Li et al. (2023) and InstructBLIP Dai et al. (2023) align visual features with language models, while LLaVA Liu et al. (2023b) and Qwen2.5-VL Bai et al. (2025) show strong instruction-following multimodal generation. Agentic parsing is also studied in ParseFixer Yu et al. (2026), which applies selective correction to backbone Markdown outputs, and ParseBench Zhang et al. (2026), which evaluates agent-relevant parsing capabilities on enterprise documents.

2.3 Visual Descriptions and Accessibility

Accessibility work shows why visual description cannot be reduced to generic captioning. Conceptual Captions Sharma et al. (2018) demonstrates the scale available in web alt text, but weakly tied to accessibility intent. VizWiz Gurari et al. (2018) and VizWiz-Captions Gurari et al. (2020) foreground blind-user scenarios, where the useful answer depends on context. TextCaps Sidorov et al. (2020) shows that descriptions may depend on visible text, and OCR-VQA Mishra et al. (2019) makes text reading part of visual question answering. Screen2Words Wang et al. (2021a) shifts the target to UI screens, while Alt-Text with Context Srivatsan et al. (2024) conditions descriptions on surrounding social text. Furthermore, ChartQA Masry et al. (2022) requires visual and logical reasoning, and DePlot Liu et al. (2023a) recovers chart data before reasoning. Chart-to-Text Kantharaj et al. (2022) directly studies chart description, while PlotQA Methani et al. (2020) emphasizes quantitative plot understanding. A useful description must be tied to the correct object, caption, page position, and surrounding reading flow. Read-Parse-Describe therefore evaluates alternative text as a field in the parse rather than as an isolated captioning output.

3 Read-Parse-Describe Dataset

3.1 Task Definition

We introduce the Read-Parsing-Describe, a dataset for document parsing with grounded visual description. This task is motivated by two limitations of existing document understanding benchmarks as shown in Tab. 1. First, many layout datasets primarily focus on the physical localization of page regions but do not require models to recover a complete logic-aware document representation. This limitation is especially pronounced in scientific papers, where frequently break simple top-to-bottom ordering rules. Second, visual elements are often treated as layout categories rather than semantic objects. Figures, charts, diagrams, screenshots may be localized, but the information they convey is rarely required to be presented in a grounded, accessible form.

3.2 Output Schema

Read-Parsing-Describe therefore evaluates document understanding as a unified multi-modal parsing problem. The target output is an ordered list of document elements. Each element contains its bounding box, semantic category, reading-order index, recognized content when applicable, caption linkage, and visual description when applicable:

Y=[e1,e2,…,en],Y=[e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}], (1)

where each element is represented as

ei={id,bbox,category,order,text,html,caption_id,alt_text},e_{i}=\{\texttt{id},\texttt{bbox},\texttt{category},\texttt{order},\texttt{text},\texttt{html},\texttt{caption\_id},\texttt{alt\_text}\}, (2)

where id is the element identifier, bbox is a page-coordinate box [x1,y1,x2,y2][x_{1},y_{1},x_{2},y_{2}] in the rendered image coordinate system. category is the semantic layout label, and order is the canonical human reading-order index. The submitted list is expected to be sorted by order, i.e., if list position and order disagree, evaluation first normalizes by the order field and leaves duplicate or missing indices to be penalized by matching and sequence metrics. text stores recognized text for textual regions, html stores table structure, caption_id links a visual object to caption, and alt_text stores a factual visual description. Non-applicable fields are set to null.

Terminology.

An ordered schema is the full element list YY after sorting by the reading-order index. The central design choice is to make fields agree inside the same element object, not to score familiar subtasks in isolation. The contract has four coupled decisions:

Coupling Design reason Failure exposed
Element identity Bind id, category, textual content, caption links, and descriptions to the same object. Free-floating OCR, HTML, captions, or descriptions cannot be credited without the element they claim to describe.
Geometry as evidence Treat bbox as the audit handle for text, tables, and visual descriptions. A plausible description or table string attached to the wrong crop becomes measurable rather than silently accepted.
Canonical reading flow Use order as human reading order rather than visual-nearest-neighbor order. Two-column text, spanning figures, and separated captions expose sequence errors even when OCR is correct.
Caption semantics Require caption_id and alt_text for visual instances when applicable. A model must bind the object, caption, and description instead of generating generic image captions.

The couplings above make the task a test of spatially grounded binding. Region proposals decide the visual evidence available to OCR, table serialization, caption linkage, and alt-text generation. Reading-order decisions decide where captions and objects sit in the page narrative; and visual descriptions are auditable only when their evidence is localized.

3.3 Dataset Creation Pipeline

We collect open-access PDF papers from the ACM Digital Library and retain document metadata. Since the main contributions, core figures, methods, and experimental results of scientific papers are usually concentrated in the main body, we extract the first eight pages of each paper and keep shorter papers in their entirety. This page-level curation strategy preserves structurally and semantically informative regions of papers while reducing the dominance of long reference sections and appendices. To focus annotation on the dense parts of papers while reducing long reference sections, we retain the first eight pages of each paper and keep shorter papers in full. Additional detailed dataset statistics would be included in the technical appendix.

The visual elements include tables, diagrams, screenshots, photographs, charts, and long-tail illustrations. This diversity matters because visual-description generation is not the same problem for each object type, e.g., a UI screenshot requires interface semantics. The layout labels are similarly heterogeneous, covering structural headers, scholarly objects, captions, references, lists, and paragraphs. We keep these categories explicit to avoid hiding errors that make scientific PDFs hard to parse. We split at the paper level with a 90:5:5 train/validation/test ratio after deduplication. Exact duplicate PDFs are removed using SHA-256 hashes, DOI metadata is used when available, normalized titles are matched otherwise, and near-duplicate title/abstract pairs above the similarity threshold are manually inspected. Paper-level splitting is important because adjacent pages share templates, section styles, figure numbering, author metadata, and sometimes repeated visual objects. Contrast a page-level split would overstate generalization for reading order and caption linkage.

3.4 Annotation Pipeline

Annotations are produced with a bootstrap-and-correct pipeline designed around cross-field consistency. A document parser first initializes layout boxes and labels. The generated boxes, semantic categories, caption links, and reading-order indices are then manually inspected and corrected together, rather than as independent layers. Corrections target common scientific-PDF failure modes: two-column reading order, spanning figures, captions separated from visual objects, footnotes, equations, author metadata, and fine-grained heading levels. This joint correction step is important: moving a box can change its text crop, its caption candidate, and its reading-order position.

Visual instances then receive alternative-text annotations through a triage loop: generate an initial description, score it against the accessibility rubric, refine low-score cases by human review, and audit the revised labels. Gemini 3 Pro Google DeepMind (2025b) provides the initial descriptions and Gemini 3 Flash Google DeepMind (2025a) scores factual accuracy, completeness, and prompt adherence on a 1–5 scale. The 1,408 descriptions scoring below 4 are routed to human refinement, then re-scored:

After refinement, the score-5 rate increases from 66.2% to 98.1%. A manual audit of 200 revised samples with previous scores below 5 gives 194/200 exact agreement between human and LLM scores. The technical appendix includes the prompt, scoring rubric, full score distribution, and audit matrix for this annotation stage.

The alt-text process is designed for benchmark consistency, not as an automatic accessibility deployment pipeline. The prompt asks for concise factual descriptions and discourages speculation beyond visible evidence. The scoring step checks whether the description is faithful, complete enough for the object type, and aligned with the prompt; human refinement is concentrated on low-score cases because these are most likely to contain missing relationships, hallucinated labels, or vague descriptions. We expose this procedure because visual-description labels are harder to audit than boxes or OCR strings, and the reader should be able to separate measured model behavior from annotation assumptions.

4 SARA: Spatial Alignment Residual Adapter

Read-Parse-Describe turns parsing into a binding problem, i.e., each generated element must keep the attribute attached to the same page evidence. This creates a different pressure from ordinary VLM generation. A visual concatenation is useful due to the compression of image tokens into a sequence the decoder can consume, but that compression can blur the local spatial cues needed to decide where an element starts, how two-column regions should be ordered, and which caption belongs to which object. The design goal of SARA is therefore not to replace the base VLM, but to restore crop-level spatial evidence at the point where the decoder receives merged visual tokens. The key design choice is to preserve correspondence between each crop’s pre-merger grid and its native post-merger tokens, enabling aligned feature re-injection without ground-truth input boxes.

5 Method

SARA follow threefold design as shown in the Fig. 1: (1) Reuse intermediate visual states rather than only the final merged tokens, because earlier layers retain finer layout and boundary information. (2) Align the reused states to the same crop grid as the native visual merger, so the residual signal has the same token-level support as the decoder’s original visual stream. (3) Inject the aligned guidance through a learnable residual gate, preserving the pretrained visual-language pathway while letting training decide how much spatial correction is useful.

Multi-layer spatial features.

Let 𝒮={2,5,8,11}\mathcal{S}=\{2,5,8,11\} be the selected visual encoder layers. During the forward pass, hooks collect hidden states

𝑿(l)∈ℝLv×dv,l∈𝒮,\bm{X}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{v}\times d_{v}},\quad l\in\mathcal{S}, (3)

where LvL_{v} is the pre-merger visual-token length and dvd_{v} is the visual feature dimension. We concatenate these states along the channel dimension:

𝑿cat=Concat⁡(𝑿(2),𝑿(5),𝑿(8),𝑿(11)).\bm{X}_{\mathrm{cat}}=\operatorname{Concat}\left(\bm{X}^{(2)},\bm{X}^{(5)},\bm{X}^{(8)},\bm{X}^{(11)}\right). (4)

The concatenated feature is mapped to the merger dimension dmd_{m} by a small projector,

𝑮=𝑾2​σ​(LN⁡(𝑾1​𝑿cat)),\bm{G}=\bm{W}_{2}\,\sigma\left(\operatorname{LN}(\bm{W}_{1}\bm{X}_{\mathrm{cat}})\right), (5)

where LN\operatorname{LN} is LayerNorm and σ\sigma is GELU.

Crop-aware alignment.

The visual merger reduces spatial resolution, so the guidance 𝑮\bm{G} must be aligned with the native merged tokens. For each crop with grid metadata (ti,hi,wi)(t_{i},h_{i},w_{i}), we slice the corresponding segment from 𝑮\bm{G}, reshape it into its two-dimensional grid, and average-pool to the merged-grid resolution:

𝑮i′=Pool2​D⁡(Reshape⁡(𝑮i),(hi/2,wi/2)).\bm{G}_{i}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Pool}_{2D}\left(\operatorname{Reshape}(\bm{G}_{i}),(h_{i}/2,w_{i}/2)\right). (6)

All crop-level features are flattened and concatenated into 𝑮′∈ℝLm×dm\bm{G}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{m}\times d_{m}}, matching the length and dimension of the original merged visual tokens TT.

Residual injection.

The enhanced visual tokens are

𝑻^=𝑻+λ​𝑮′,\hat{\bm{T}}=\bm{T}+\lambda\bm{G}^{\prime}, (7)

where λ\lambda is a learnable scalar gate initialized to 1.0. The language decoder then generates the same ordered schema used by all baselines. SARA changes only the visual token pathway; it does not alter the benchmark labels, target schema, or evaluation metrics.

Shape summary and scope.

The data flow is 𝑿(l)∈ℝLv×dv\bm{X}^{(l)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{v}\times d_{v}}, 𝑿cat∈ℝLv×|𝒮|​dv\bm{X}_{\mathrm{cat}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{v}\times|\mathcal{S}|d_{v}}, 𝑮∈ℝLv×dm\bm{G}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{v}\times d_{m}}, and 𝑮′,𝑻,𝑻^∈ℝLm×dm\bm{G}^{\prime},\bm{T},\hat{\bm{T}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{m}\times d_{m}} after crop-aware pooling. SARA is not intended to replace document-specific supervision or table-aware decoding. The residual form keeps the original visual-token stream intact and lets training learn the aligned guidance.

6 Experiments

6.1 Settings and Metrics

We evaluate three categories of systems: general-purpose VLMs, specialized document models, and pipeline parsers. General-purpose VLMs include Qwen3.5 Qwen Team (2026), Gemma4 Google DeepMind (2026c), ChatGPT-5.4 OpenAI (2026b), ChatGPT-5.6 OpenAI (2026a), Gemini 3.6 Flash Google DeepMind (2026b) and Gemini 3.1 Pro Google DeepMind (2026a). Specialized document models include DeepSeek-OCR Wei et al. (2025), DeepSeek-OCR2 Wei et al. (2026), Dolphin-v2 Feng et al. (2026), MonkeyOCR Li et al. (2025), VGT Da et al. (2023), GOT-OCR 2.0 Wei et al. (2024), Nougat Blecher et al. (2023), and PaddleOCR-VL Cui et al. (2025a). Pipeline parsers include PP-StructureV3 Cui et al. (2025b) and MinerU Wang et al. (2024).

All systems are evaluated under the same page-level output schema. Zero-shot systems use released checkpoints or official APIs without in-context examples. Full fine-tuning baselines serialize each target element list into text and optimize the standard autoregressive next-token objective on the training split. The validation split is used for model selection, and final results are reported on the held-out test split. For SARA runs, the base VLM is frozen and only the adapter pathway is trained. For generative VLMs, we use deterministic decoding whenever supported. Outputs from pipeline systems are converted into the unified schema.

Metrics.

All metrics are computed after schema conversion. Minor syntax errors are repaired deterministically; if a prediction remains unparsable, the affected fields are treated as empty. F1 follows the IoU-matching convention used by PubLayNet Zhong et al. (2019), DocLayNet Pfitzmann et al. (2022), and RoDLA Chen et al. (2024): a match requires the same category label and IoU≥0.5\operatorname{IoU}\geq 0.5. mIoU is computed over matched true positives. Reading-order (RO) score uses normalized edit-distance similarity over matched element identifiers Wang et al. (2021b). OCR accuracy is computed as normalized character-level edit-distance similarity after text normalization. For visual descriptions, we report METEOR Banerjee and Lavie (2005) and BERTScore Zhang et al. (2020).

6.2 Main Results

Table 2 should be read as a contract diagnostic, not a leaderboard. The unified schema requires models to jointly recover localized elements, reading order, textual content, and visual descriptions. Pipeline parsers often retain strong OCR or localization performance, but they usually leave caption links and alt-text fields incomplete. General-purpose VLMs can produce richer schema fields, but they are less reliable in spatial grounding without adaptation. Document-specialized VLMs and SARA are complementary: the former excel at specialized parsing, while SARA improves the structural fields of a frozen general-purpose VLM and maintains competitive visual-description quality.

Table 2 reveals different strengths across the evaluated systems and reported metrics. Fine-tuned Dolphin-v2 achieves the strongest localization performance, reaching 0.9826 F1 and 0.9588 mIoU. It also obtains the highest RO score, 0.9857. Fine-tuned DeepSeek-OCR achieves the highest METEOR, 0.3998, while GPT-5.6 achieves the highest BERTScore, 0.9004. DeepSeek-OCR also maintains a high RO score of 0.9825. Among the evaluated proprietary zero-shot models, GPT-5.6 obtains the highest F1, RO, and description scores, while Gemini 3.6 Flash obtains the highest mIoU. Including Gemini 3.1 Pro extends the comparison to the requested Pro-series model under the same schema. These results suggest that spatially precise parsing and open-ended visual description remain partially distinct capabilities.

Pipeline parsers remain competitive on some low-level fields but are less complete under the unified output schema. For example, MinerU reaches 0.9671 OCR accuracy and 0.9151 mIoU, but its RO score is 0.6757, and it does not produce visual alternative text under the evaluated schema. This does not mean that pipeline systems are ineffective. Instead, it identifies the fields that require additional modules or tighter integration when the target is a complete accessible page parse.

Compared with the Qwen3.5-2B full fine-tuning baseline, SARA substantially improves structural performance while keeping the base VLM frozen and training with 83.99M parameters. F1 increases to 0.9189, mIoU to 0.8919, OCR accuracy to 0.9636, and RO score to 0.9774. Its alt-text scores, 0.3834 METEOR and 0.8946 BERTScore, are also competitive with the strongest fine-tuned document VLMs. On Gemma4-E4B, SARA also improves F1 and mIoU relative to full fine-tuning, but RO and both description metrics decrease slightly. Compared with LoRA-only adaptation, SARA improves F1 and mIoU by 0.2185 and 0.2074 on Qwen and 0.1750 and 0.1898 on Gemma, respectively. Other metrics show trade-offs: Qwen LoRA has higher OCR accuracy, while Gemma LoRA has higher RO and slightly higher BERTScore.

Interpreting the joint table.

The main result is not that one model is uniformly best, but that single-axis strengths do not necessarily imply a coherent page parse. A model with high OCR but low RO may still fail to recover columns or reading sequences. A model with strong F1 but no alt-text may be useful as a front end, but it is incomplete as an accessible parser. Conversely, a model with strong alt-text but weak mIoU may describe objects that are poorly localized. Reporting these fields side by side makes such tradeoffs visible without imposing a deployment-specific ranking.

6.3 Ablations and Analysis

Table 4 isolates the contribution of each SARA component on Qwen3.5-2B. The full fine-tuning row is included as a reference, while all adapter rows keep the backbone frozen. Grid alignment alone provides a modest improvement over full fine-tuning, especially for RO and OCR. In contrast, projector-only training underperforms full fine-tuning, indicating that the gains do not come merely from adding trainable parameters. The full configuration, which combines grid-aware alignment with projector training, produces the largest improvement across all four structural metrics.

Table 4 studies which visual feature layers are most useful for the adapter. Early-to-mid layers, {2,5,8,11}, outperform both shallow-only layers and late-layer selections. This pattern is consistent with the design goal of preserving local spatial cues while retaining sufficient semantic abstraction for document elements. On both tested backbones, SARA improves localization relative to full fine-tuning, while its effects on reading order and description similarity vary. Overall, these ablations suggest that SARA primarily acts as a spatial-structure adapter rather than as a general-purpose language-generation module. This also explains why alt-text improvements are more mixed than the localization and reading-order gains.

Training-data scale.

On Qwen3.5-2B, SARA trails full fine-tuning on all four structural metrics at 10% training data and yields mixed results at 30%, while its structural advantage emerges at 50% and 100%. The complete comparison is reported in Appendix E.

6.4 Qualitative Results

Figure 2 compares annotation mapping results from the ground truth, the base Qwen3.5-2B model, full fine-tuning, and SARA. The base model often produces incomplete or poorly grounded mappings. Full fine-tuning improves schema compliance, but spatial alignment errors can remain. In comparison, SARA produces element mappings that are more consistent with the ground-truth page structure, especially for localized regions and their associated schema fields.

7 Conclusion

We introduced Read-Parse-Describe, a unified benchmark for scientific-document parsing, and SARA, a spatial adapter tailored to the same page-level output contract. The task jointly evaluates localized elements, labels, reading order, textual and table content, caption links, and alternative text within a single ordered parse. Experiments show that existing systems tend to fail different parts in evaluation, while frozen-backbone SARA tuning substantially improves structural parsing for a general VLM.

Limitations. Read-Parse-Describe is limited to open-access ACM scientific PDFs and primarily covers the first eight pages, leaving late appendices and references underrepresented. Alt-text annotations rely on LLM assistance with human refinement, and closed-source pre-training exposure cannot be fully excluded. The benchmark is intended to support accessible document understanding, search, and document mining, but generated accessibility metadata should not be treated as deployment-ready without further validation.

Appendix A Dataset Details

This appendix is supplementary reading. The main text defines the task contract and reports the primary experimental conclusions; the material below gives the distributional and procedural detail needed to inspect the benchmark more closely.

A.1 Label Taxonomy and Corpus Profile

Read-Parse-Describe uses a 23-label taxonomy rather than a small generic layout set. The goal is to keep elements that matter for reading order, reflow, caption linkage, and auditability visible as distinct targets. Headings, paragraph fragments, captions, equations, code blocks, metadata, references, lists, and visual objects therefore remain separately labeled.

The benchmark itself contains 2,402 curated scientific documents and 18,164 continuous pages. The domain chart below summarizes the broader analyzed source-corpus pool of 2,151 ACM articles from 2020–2024; the residual slice groups domains that were not individually named in the figure.

A.2 Page Curation and Element Distributions

The first-eight-page rule is intended to increase the density of multimodal scientific content while keeping each paper as a continuous page sequence. It preserves the early-paper regions where abstracts, methods, figures, tables, captions, equations, and author metadata interact most strongly. Later pages are not treated as unimportant; they are underrepresented because they are disproportionately reference-heavy in the analyzed full-text subset.

The following tables decompose the visual and layout population from two complementary angles. Subject categories describe the broad disciplinary context of visual instances. Image types describe the visual form that the alt-text and caption-linking steps must handle. Aggregated layout groups show how much of the annotation budget is spent on document structure, metadata, scholarly objects, captions, references, and fragments.

Appendix B Alt-text Annotation Details

Visual descriptions are harder to audit than boxes or OCR strings because a fluent sentence can still be vague, hallucinated, or attached to the wrong object. We therefore separate the alt-text process into generation, rubric-based scoring, targeted human refinement, and a manual audit. The detailed prompt and rubric below are provided to make the label assumptions inspectable.

The score distribution reports the same 11,338 visual instances before and after human refinement. Low-scoring generated descriptions are revised, then re-scored under the same rubric.

Appendix C Evaluation Metric

To quantitatively assess the performance of the fine-tuned models in handling complex scholarly layouts, we employ a multi-dimensional evaluation suite. This suite covers three complementary aspects: (1) physical localization of layout elements, (2) logical sequencing of the reading flow, and (3) textual and tabular accuracy of the extracted content.(4) Accessibility Metadata Evaluation.Such a decomposition is necessary because a model can, for example, detect elements correctly but still fail to order them properly, or produce fluent text while misplacing bounding boxes.

1. Physical Layout Analysis: F1-score and mIoU

For Document Layout Analysis (DLA), we evaluate the model’s ability to correctly identify and localize structural entities (e.g., figures, tables, and section blocks).

F1-score.

We compute the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall for each label category. A detection is considered a True Positive (TP) if (i) the predicted category matches the ground-truth category and (ii) the overlap between predicted and ground-truth regions exceeds a predefined threshold (typically based on IoU). The metric is defined as:

F​1=2⋅P​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​n⋅R​e​c​a​l​lP​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​n+R​e​c​a​l​lF1=2\cdot\frac{Precision\cdot Recall}{Precision+Recall}

In practice, F1-score summarizes the trade-off between missing elements (low Recall) and producing spurious detections (low Precision).

mIoU (mean Intersection over Union).

To measure geometric localization accuracy, we compute the Intersection over Union (IoU) between each predicted bounding box BpB_{p} and the corresponding ground-truth box Bg​tB_{gt}. The mean IoU over NN matched instances is reported as:

m​I​o​U=1N​∑i=1NA​r​e​a​(Bp,i∩Bg​t,i)A​r​e​a​(Bp,i∪Bg​t,i)mIoU=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{Area(B_{p,i}\cap B_{gt,i})}{Area(B_{p,i}\cup B_{gt,i})}

Compared to F1-score, mIoU is more sensitive to precise boundary alignment, which is critical for downstream tasks such as figure-to-caption association or table cell reconstruction.

2. Logical Reading Order: Normalized Edit Distance (NED)

To evaluate Reading Order (RO), we represent the sequence of detected blocks as a string of identifiers and compare it with the ground-truth sequence. We use the Levenshtein edit distance to measure the minimal number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform the predicted order into the correct order. To ensure comparability across documents with different numbers of blocks, we normalize the distance and define the RO score as:

R​OS​c​o​r​e=1−L​e​v​e​n​s​h​t​e​i​n​(Sp,Sg​t)max⁡(|Sp|,|Sg​t|)RO_{Score}=1-\frac{Levenshtein(S_{p},S_{gt})}{\max(|S_{p}|,|S_{gt}|)}

where SpS_{p} and Sg​tS_{gt} denote the predicted and ground-truth block sequences, respectively. A higher score indicates a more faithful logical flow, which is essential for reflowable rendering and accessible reading.

3. Textual and Tabular Accuracy: ED and TEDS

OCR accuracy (Edit Distance, ED).

For general text extraction, we compute character-level edit distance between the recognized text and the reference transcription. This metric directly reflects transcription fidelity and is particularly informative for scientific documents containing symbols, subscripts, and uncommon terminology.

Table reconstruction (TEDS).

For table parsing, we use the Tree Edit Distance Based Similarity (TEDS), which evaluates both the global structure (row/column organization) and the cell content by representing tables as tree structures. The similarity is defined as:

T​E​D​S​(Ta,Tb)=1−D​i​s​tt​r​e​e​(Ta,Tb)max⁡(|Ta|,|Tb|)TEDS(T_{a},T_{b})=1-\frac{Dist_{tree}(T_{a},T_{b})}{\max(|T_{a}|,|T_{b}|)}

where TaT_{a} and TbT_{b} are the predicted and ground-truth table trees. This metric is more aligned with human judgment than plain text metrics, because it penalizes structural errors (e.g., merged/split cells) in addition to textual mistakes.

4. Accessibility Metadata Evaluation: METEOR Score

To evaluate the quality of the generated Alt-text for figures and tables, we employ the METEOR metric. While metrics like BLEU primarily focus on exact n-gram overlaps, METEOR is designed to capture the semantic nuances of scholarly descriptions more effectively.

The Rationale for Choosing METEOR

In the context of academic document reconstruction, the description of a figure (Alt-text) can be linguistically diverse. METEOR is superior for this task due to its unique features:Synonym Matching: It utilizes a dictionary (like WordNet) to match synonyms. For instance, if the ground truth says "Diagram" and the model generates "Schematic," METEOR recognizes this as a valid match, whereas BLEU would penalize it.Stemming: It matches words with the same root (e.g., "clustering" and "clustered"), which is crucial for maintaining the technical accuracy of alt-text.Alignment-based Scoring: It creates an explicit alignment between the predicted string and the reference, penalizing incorrect word orders through a "fragmentation penalty."

Mathematical Formulation

The METEOR score is calculated by combining the harmonic mean of precision (PP) and recall (RR), with a specific emphasis on recall, followed by a penalty for incorrect ordering.First, the F-score is computed as:

Fm​e​a​n=P⋅Rα⋅P+(1−α)⋅RF_{mean}=\frac{P\cdot R}{\alpha\cdot P+(1-\alpha)\cdot R}

Typically, α\alpha is set to give more weight to recall, ensuring that the descriptive content of the figure is fully captured.Then a Penalty (P​e​nPen) is calculated based on the "chunkiness" of the alignment (how fragmented the matches are):

P​e​n=γ⋅(#​c​h​u​n​k​s#​u​n​i​g​r​a​m​s​_​m​a​t​c​h​e​d)βPen=\gamma\cdot\left(\frac{\#chunks}{\#unigrams\_matched}\right)^{\beta}

The final METEOR Score is:

S​c​o​r​e=Fm​e​a​n⋅(1−P​e​n)Score=F_{mean}\cdot(1-Pen)

Appendix D Evaluation Details

All reported systems are converted into the same element schema before scoring. Layout matching requires category agreement and an IoU threshold of 0.5. DLA-F1 is computed over matched layout elements, and mIoU averages the IoU of true-positive matches. Reading order is evaluated over matched element identifiers, so a model must both find the relevant element and place it correctly in the sequence. OCR is normalized before edit-distance scoring, and table content is scored through the serialized html field when a system produces it. Visual descriptions are scored only for visual instances with reference alternative text; a missing description for an applicable object receives zero for the description metric.

Unparsable predictions are not discarded globally. Minor syntax errors are repaired deterministically when the intended field structure is recoverable. If a prediction remains unparsable, only the affected fields are treated as empty. This localizes a syntax failure to the fields it prevents from being evaluated and avoids giving a model credit for content that cannot be reliably associated with an element object.

Appendix E Training-data Scaling

We compare full fine-tuning and SARA on Qwen3.5-2B using 10%, 30%, 50%, and 100% of the training data under the same reported evaluation protocol. Table 13 reports all six metrics. At 10%, SARA trails full fine-tuning on all four structural metrics. Results are mixed at 30%; at 50%, it improves F1, mIoU, and OCR while matching RO, and at 100% it improves all four. The F1 difference changes from −0.0756-0.0756 at 10% to +0.1790+0.1790 at 50% and +0.1853+0.1853 at 100%. Thus, the structural advantage emerges at larger training fractions in this experiment. METEOR favors the adapter at each fraction, while BERTScore changes are mixed.

Appendix F Resolution Sensitivity

We evaluate Qwen3.5-2B+SARA at 100%, 50%, and 25% of the reported native crop resolution while keeping the model and evaluation settings fixed. As shown in Table 14, reducing resolution to 25% decreases F1 by 0.1600, mIoU by 0.0725, OCR by 0.1988, and RO by 0.0910. Because mIoU is averaged over matched true positives, its remaining value describes overlap among surviving matches and does not indicate preservation of all element boundaries. This experiment measures absolute input-resolution sensitivity; it does not establish a robustness advantage over full fine-tuning without a corresponding control evaluated at the same resolutions.

Appendix G Failure cases.

To better understand the limitations of SARA, we analyze two representative failure modes, shown in Figure 4. First, borderless composite figures can confuse the model when multiple sub-figures and intra-image text are densely arranged. In such cases, visual and textual cues become entangled, which may shift predicted figure boxes away from their corresponding captions. Second, excessively dense tables can stress the decoding process. Although the table region may still be localized accurately, long serialized outputs may be truncated near the end, and the model may occasionally introduce minor irrelevant artifacts.
